Single-celled organisms
+ 1 Read the passage below and list the four main points.
If you take a drop of pond water and inspect it under a microscope, you will see some 
small shapes. Some are green and are probably single-celled plants. Some are colourless 
and move about eating other shapes. These are very simple single-celled animals called 
protozoa. Protozoa are classified into groups according to how they move. Ciliates have 
many small hairs that move in waves, making the cell move very fast. Flagellates have one 
or more long whip-like structures that thrash about, propelling the cell along. Amoebas 
move in a flowing motion, their shape changing from moment to moment. Their body 
substance flows into slender, finger-like extensions as they move.

The seven levels of classification
Traditionally, when classifying organisms, scientists sort them into groups on seven 
levels. This is known as a hierarchical system. Each level classifies the organism in more 
detail. The first, and highest, of these levels is Kingdom. Organisms can be in either the 
animal or plant kingdom, or in other kingdoms such as fungi and bacteria. 
+ 1 What kingdom would you place the following organisms in?
platypus   carrot   frog   rose  
Next, organisms are sorted by their structure. This refers to whether an animal 
has a backbone (chordata), or a soft body or a hard outer shell. This level is called the 
Phylum. 
Organisms are then sorted by Class, then Order, Family, Genus and Species. Each 
level goes into more detail about the structure, shape and other characteristics of the 
organism. The group names are in Latin or Greek, but they are often similar to common 
English names. For example, Class mammalia means mammals.

Human vs cow digestion
Human digestive systems are called monogastric systems. A cow’s digestive system is 
called a ruminant system. Ruminants have four stomachs, beginning with the rumen, then 
the reticulum, the omasum and finally the abomasum. Chewed grass stored in the rumen 
is regurgitated back into the mouth and the cow chews it again. This is called chewing the 
cud. The cud is then swallowed and passes to the reticulum.

Activity sheet – Food chains
Feral animals – Cats
Feral cats are found in all areas of Australia. They spend most of the day hiding and 
sleeping, and hunt at night. Feral cats don’t drink much water, as they get moisture from 
the animals they kill. They kill birds, small mammals, reptiles and frogs. Some larger cats 
will even kill animals the size of a possum. Feral cats hunt many native species and 
ground-nesting birds. Scientists believe they have hunted many species of small desert 
animals to extinction. Bilby, numbat and mala populations have all been seriously 
affected by the feral cat population. 
Feral cats breed throughout the year and have few predators, except dingoes and 
eagles. They are hard to control because they don’t take baits and are shy of traps. They 
avoid humans and so are hard to shoot.

The malleefowl
The malleefowl is an Australian ground-dwelling bird. 
They are shy, solitary birds who only come together to 
mate. The male malleefowl digs a big hole in the ground 
and fills it with organic material such as sticks, bark and 
leaves. He then waits for rain. Once the organic matter is 
damp, he covers it with a thick layer of sand. The organic 
matter begins to decompose and generates heat. Every 
day the male checks the mound’s temperature by poking 
his bill into it. When it is warm enough, the female lays her eggs inside the mound. Then 
she leaves the site and the male bird tends the mound daily, maintaining the internal 
temperature at 33°C. He does this by scraping away or adding the insulating sand. 
The eggs take 7–9 weeks to incubate. By this time the male bird has stopped 
maintaining the mound and has left the hatchlings to fend for themselves. The chicks hatch 
inside the mound and struggle their way out of the sand. They never know their parents.

Echolocation
Ghost bats live in northern Australia and are Australia’s only carnivorous bat species. 
Ghost bats have long, large ears that are very sensitive to sound. They use echolocation 
to hunt at night for large insects, lizards, birds, frogs and small bats. Used by many bat 
species, echolocation involves using sound waves to locate food and find their way 
around in the dark.
The sound waves bounce back from animals and objects around the bats. They listen 
for the returning waves to work out the size, location and direction of movement of 
animals nearby. If the waves return quickly, they know the animal is close by. If the sound 
waves are intense, this tells them that the animal is large. If the waves return first to the 
bat’s left ear, then moments later to its right ear, this means the animal is on their left.

DNA discoveries
DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is found in the nuclei of cells and contains 
genetic material called genes. Since the 1940s scientists have known that DNA is the 
molecule of life, but they didn’t know what the molecule looked like. They knew DNA 
consisted of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). These 
bases joined together in pairs; A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. Scientists 
also knew that the structure had a phosphate backbone but they weren’t sure how the 
bases formed along it. In 1953 two scientists named Watson and Crick proposed that the 
bases are paired like rungs in a twisted ladder that attaches to the phosphate backbone. 
The formation is called a double helix.

Mendel’s pea plants (1)
Gregor Mendel bred pea plants to study the laws of heredity. 
Peas grow quickly and there are many types. Mendel chose 
a pure line of tall peas to cross pollinate with a pure line 
of dwarf peas. He called the seeds from this pairing the F1 
(first generation) plants, or the F1 generation. They were 
called hybrids because they grew from a cross between two 
genetically different plants. All the F1 plants were tall. 
 
l Mendel said that tallness dominated ‘dwarfness’. 
 
l Mendel called the tall gene T and the dwarf gene t. 
Next, Mendel pollinated all the F1 plants with one another. 
He collected their seeds and planted them. The plants that 
grew were called the F2 plants or F2 generation. Some F2 plants 
were dwarf but many were tall. From this, Mendel concluded that dwarfness was caused 
by a recessive gene.
Punnet squares are drawn up to predict the phenotype of individuals from a 
genetic cross.
 
l The genotype refers to the individual’s genes.
 
l The phenotype refers to the individual’s appearance.

Dasyurids vs kangaroos
Genetic diversity is a term used to describe the variety of genes within any species. 
Some animals such as kangaroos are all genetically very similar. Dasyurids, or carnivorous 
marsupials, have evolved from ancient species and are more genetically diverse. Numbats, 
quolls and the Tasmanian devil are all dasyurids. If one species of dasyurid becomes 
extinct, we lose a large genetic resource. Several species of dasyurids are endangered 
and the Tasmanian Tiger is already extinct.

though they cover a small amount of the Earth’s surface, they support a large amount of 
its biodiversity. Australia also provides many different climatic conditions and habitats.

range of species.

Plant diseases
Like animals, plants also suffer from disease. Fungal diseases such as mildew and 
brown rot are common in vegetable and fruit crops. The fungus spreads from plant to 
plant through tiny fungal spores which float in the air. The spores thrive in warm, moist 
conditions. Bacterial diseases such as bacterial blight are also airborne and thrive in 
humid crowded conditions, such as among potted glasshouse plants. Plant diseases are

Ross River virus
Many diseases are spread by contact between people but some are spread by vectors. 
Vectors are disease-carrying organisms. The mosquito is a common vector that can spread 
serious diseases such as malaria and dengue fever. In Australia the Ross River virus is 
spread by mosquitoes. The virus mostly infects people in rural areas, and causes a flu-like 
illness with a rash, joint pains and fever. Sometimes joints can become swollen. The illness 
can last for several weeks, making the patient feel weak and tired. Fortunately it is not fatal, 
but there is no specific treatment.

Vaccinations
Vaccines are liquids that contain either dead germ particles or harmless live germs. The 
germs used to make a vaccine are similar to the germs that cause the disease being 
vaccinated against. When a vaccine enters the bloodstream, the body reacts as if it were 
actually suffering from an infection and makes antibodies. The antibodies stay in the 
blood for a long time, making the body immune to a real infection. 
Scientists have produced vaccines for a range of deadly diseases such as tetanus, 
diphtheria and measles. Most vaccinations are injected but some, such as the polio 
vaccine, are swallowed.

Activity sheet – Natural selection
Isolated islands
When Charles Darwin studied finch populations in the remote Galapagos Islands, he 
noticed that the island finches had different shaped beaks to the mainland finches from 
which they were descended. The mainland finches’ beaks were suited to eating grain, which 
was scarce on the islands. The island finches’ beaks were better suited to eating insects, fruit 
or leaves. Darwin believed that over many generations, island finches with diverse beak 
shapes survived better than those whose beaks were the same as the mainland finches. 
Darwin proposed that the finches that had adapted so they could eat a variety of 
foods, rather than depending on the limited supplies of grain, survived and passed on 
their characteristics to their young. Because the finches were isolated, the genetic base 
was small and the beak characteristics of the mainland finches were bred out over time. 
Darwin described the survival of those species that changed their characteristics in order 
to survive as natural selection.

Crown-of-thorns starfish
Crown-of-thorns starfish are large starfish that eat coral polyps. In some years large 
outbreaks of the starfish occur on Australia’s greatest tourist attraction, the Great Barrier 
Reef. The females produce approximately 60 million eggs a year. The eggs drift for months 
in the water as zooplankton, feeding on microscopic algae. In an outbreak year more of 
the eggs reach maturity because more nutrients have washed into the sea, creating more 
algae for the zooplankton to eat.  
Once they grow larger they settle on coral. Adult starfish can reach 30 cm in diameter. 
They are covered in sharp poisonous spines that can pierce clothing. A single starfish can 
move up to 20 m per hour, searching for food, and in a year they can eat around 6 m2 of 
living coral reef. As adults they have few predators.

Monitoring populations
To compare populations biologists need to look at densities. Density refers to the number 
of individuals of a species per unit area. For instance, species such as kangaroos and weeds 
can be counted on a per hectare basis. However, it’s not possible to count every individual 
in a population. Individual animals can move or be hidden from view and some weeds grow 
in clumps or from underground shoots. To combat this, animals can be counted per nesting 
site or burrow. Clumping plants can be counted as the total weight of the population per 
unit area. Insects and microorganisms might be best expressed as number of individuals 
per unit of volume. For example water bugs could be counted per litre of pond water.

Plant responses to temperature 
+ 1 Read the information below, then underline any examples of how plants 
respond to temperature changes.
Oranges grown in cool regions have green skin while their fruit forms in the hot summer 
months. In autumn when the fruit ripens, the skin colour changes to orange. This colour 
change is due to the cooling air temperature. Ripe oranges grown in tropical climates 
normally stay green-skinned because there are no cooler months. 
Plants are very sensitive to temperature changes and day length. Deciduous trees 
lose their leaves in autumn when the temperature drops and days are shorter. The trees 
become dormant and their sap doesn’t flow. In countries where snowfall is frequent 
this leaf-fall and dormancy protects the trees from freezing. Bulbs such as tulips flower 
best when they have been through a period of chilling, as if packed under snow. In 
Australia these conditions are rare so commercial growers ‘force’ tulips into flowering by 
refrigerating them for several months.

Prehistoric plants
The earliest plants on Earth were marine algae that lived billions of 
years ago. During the Silurian period plants appeared on land. They 
were leafless vascular plants called psilophytes. Early mosses also 
appeared around the same time. The next plants to evolve were ferns 
and conifers, cycads and gingkoes. Many dinosaurs ate these species. 
Flowering plants and grasses are relatively modern in geological time. 
They developed during the Cretaceous period.

Resource sheet – Atoms and elements
The periodic table (1)
Elements such as carbon, gold and copper have been known since ancient times. 
Hydrogen was discovered in 1766. By 1800, scientists had started sorting the elements 
into groups. At that time many elements had not yet been discovered. In 1869, a Russian 
scientist named Dimitri Mendeleev ordered the elements according to how heavy they 
were. He displayed this information in a chart and called it the periodic table.
Look at the periodic table on the inside front cover of this book. The periodic table 
contains more than 100 elements, but only 92 of them are found naturally on earth. 
The rest are man-made. Elements that have similar properties are grouped together in 
columns in the table. For example, helium (He) has similar properties to neon (Ne) – both 
are gases that do not react – so they are grouped together.
The elements grouped on the left-hand side of the periodic table are metals.  
The non-metals are grouped on the right-hand side.
Each element has a chemical symbol. Some symbols have one letter, while others have 
two or three. For example, C is the symbol for carbon. Chlorine, which was discovered 
after carbon, has the symbol Cl. Some symbols come from the element’s Latin name. The 
symbol for iron is Fe, which comes from its Latin name, Ferrum.

Activity sheet – Chemical reactions
Reactants and products
When a chemical reaction occurs, new substances are made. The substances that we start 
with are called the reactants. The new substances that are made are called the products. 
The properties of the products are different from the properties of the reactants. 
We can describe what happens in a chemical reaction by writing a word equation.
reactants

so that you do not mix up the reactants and products.

Resource sheet – Compounds
Joining elements (1)
In some elements, such as oxygen, the atoms pair up. A particle that is made up of more 
than one atom is called a molecule. We can show this using the chemical symbols for the 
atoms involved. For example, oxygen molecules can be represented as O2. The number in 
the formula shows how many atoms of the type there are in the molecule. 
We can represent molecules by drawing coloured circles to show the atoms. When 
we draw a molecule we draw the atoms of that type touching, to show that they are 
chemically joined together.
Element
Formula for  
molecule

oxygen – a non-metal gas

When two or more atoms from different elements join together, they form a compound. 
The formula for a compound shows the types of elements that are in the compound and 
the ratio (how many atoms of each element there are). 
Carbon dioxide is a compound made up of carbon and oxygen. It has the formula:
Carbon atom
Oxygen atoms
CO2
C is the symbol for carbon
There are two oxygen atoms
O is the symbol for oxygen
This formula tells us that a molecule of carbon dioxide is always made  
up of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. We don’t need to add  
a one after carbon. A chemical formula only includes a number after  
an element symbol if there is more than one atom of that element.

Activity sheet – Matter
Materials and their uses
The ways a material can be used depend on its properties. 
• A saucepan is usually made out of metal and plastic. Metal is used because it is a good 
conductor of heat. Plastic is used for the handle because plastic is an insulator, or poor 
conductor of heat. This stops you burning your hand when you pick up the saucepan. 
• Electrical cables are often made out of a metal called copper because it is a good 
conductor of electricity and can easily be formed into wires. The copper wire is 
surrounded with a plastic covering so the electrical cable can be handled safely. 
• Ceramic materials are used for lots of different things. Traditional ceramics are used to 
make dishes and tiles because they are hard, do not absorb liquid and are both heat 
and rust resistant. Space shuttles have tiles made from ceramics because they protect 
the shuttle from extreme temperatures. 
Scientists are always trying to design better or smarter materials to develop new 
technology and improve the way objects work. Smart materials are able to respond to 
changes in the environment.

Activity sheet – Matter
Measuring matter
Matter takes up space. This means that it has volume. Volume is one measurement of 
matter. You can use a formula to calculate the volume of regular-shaped objects. You can 
also measure the volume of an object by dropping it in water and calculating the amount 
of water it displaces, or pushes aside. 
Mass is another measurement of matter. Mass describes the amount of matter or atoms 
in a substance. Matter can be measured by finding the weight of an object. An object’s 
weight depends on its mass and how much gravity is pulling on it. For example, an object 
weighs less on the moon than on earth because there is less gravity on the moon. We can 
use a spring balance to measure weight. 
The density of an object depends on both its mass and its volume. Objects with tightly 
packed atoms are very dense. Objects with atoms spaced further apart are less dense. Density 
is measured in grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm3) or kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3).

Properties of non-metals
 
Non-metals have the opposite characteristics to metals. For example, 
metals are shiny but non-metals are dull. Non-metals:
• do not conduct heat and electricity very well
• are brittle (this means they may shatter if you hit them)
• are usually dull
• have low melting and boiling points
• are usually gases at room temperature
• are light for their size
• are softer and weaker than metals
• can be solids, but only bromine is a liquid at room temperature.

Resource sheet – Physical and chemical changes
Changing matter
Changes to matter can be classified as either physical or chemical changes. During a 
physical change some of the characteristics of the substance change, but the substance 
remains the same. No new substance is formed.
When we boil water, it changes into steam. Steam is another form of water. When water is 
heated, this does not create a new substance – it simply changes the water’s state from a 
liquid to a gas. Examples of physical changes to matter include: 
• changes of state (solid, liquid, gas)
• changes in shape or size
• dissolving.
Physical changes are usually easy to change back, or reverse. For example, if you dissolve 
salt in water, you can separate the salt back out by boiling the water.
When a chemical change occurs, the original substance is changed into something new. 
A chemical change is caused by a chemical reaction. A chemical change is irreversible –  
you cannot get the original substance back. For example, when a candle is lit, some of 
the wax melts, which is a physical change, and some of it burns and changes to ash and 
smoke, which is a chemical change. 
To identify that a chemical change has taken place, we can look for 
the following clues:
• The substance fizzes or bubbles (gas is produced).
• Smoke is produced.
• Heat is produced.
• Light energy is produced (the substance glows, or a flame is produced).
• You cannot get the original substance back.
• There is a permanent colour change.
• There is a smell.
• A solid forms when two liquids are mixed.

Evaporation and crystallisation
Filtration cannot be used to separate substances that have been dissolved in a solvent, 
because the particles are too small and pass through the filter paper. Heat can be used 
to separate a liquid from a solution, leaving the solute behind. This process is called 
evaporation.
+

Filtration is used to remove (soluble/insoluble) substances from a liquid.
Evaporation is used to remove (soluble/insoluble) substances from a liquid.
When you separate a solution using evaporation, you (keep/lose) the solvent.
When you separate a solution using evaporation, you are left with the (solute/solvent).
Evaporating the water from a solution by heating is a quick method of separating the 
solute from the solvent. However, sometimes evaporation is not a suitable method 
because the quantities are too large, or you want large crystals. In these cases, 
crystallisation can be used instead. For example, in the production of commercial salt,  
the sun’s heat is used to evaporate the water. Large salt crystals form because the water  
is evaporated slowly.

Filtration
Filtration is used to separate a mixture of an insoluble solid and a liquid. The mixture is 
poured through filter paper. Only the liquid passes through – this is called the filtrate.  
The solid that is collected on the filter paper is called the residue.

Resource sheet – Solids, liquids and gases
The particle model of matter (1)
There are three states of matter: solid, liquid and gas. The particle model is a scientific 
explanation that describes the differences between each state. When we imagine particles 
in the three states of matter, it is as if we are looking at objects with a very powerful 
microscope and seeing what is happening inside them.
Solids
The particles in solids:
• are very close together
• are tightly held together
• have a small amount of energy
• can only move by vibrating.
Because of this, solids: 
• are heavy
• have a definite shape
• do not flow easily
• are hard to compress.
Liquids
The particles in liquids: 
• are close together
• are weakly held together
• have a larger amount  
of energy
• vibrate, but can also slide  
over each other and  
change places.
Because of this, liquids:
• are heavy
• can be poured or  
flow freely
• have no definite shape
• fill the shape of  
a container
• can’t be compressed.
Gases
The particles in gases: 
• are spread far apart
• are free from each other
• have a large amount of  
energy
• move around quickly and  
freely in all directions.
Because of this, gases:
• are light
• can change shape
• flow freely
• do not have a definite  
shape or volume
• spread out to fill  
a container
• can be compressed.

Activity sheet – Solids, liquids and gases
What is diffusion?
Diffusion occurs when particles move from where there are lots of particles (high 
concentration) to where there are fewer particles (low concentration). Solids cannot diffuse 
because their particles are too close together and are strongly attracted to each other. Liquids 
and gases are able to diffuse. Gases diffuse the quickest because their particles are free to 
move quickly in different directions. When a liquid or gas is heated, it diffuses more quickly. 
+

an area where there is (more/less) of the substance to an area where there is (more/less). 
Gases diffuse (quickly/slowly) because the particles are moving quickly in all directions. 
Liquids can also diffuse but the particles move more (slowly/quickly). 
Solid particles cannot diffuse because they cannot move, they can only (vibrate/slide 
over each other). An odour is a (gas/liquid) that is given off by a substance. You can smell 
perfume because the scent particles diffuse through the air to your nose in the form of 
a (solid/gas). If you drop a little bit of dye into a jar of water the colour will spread slowly 
through the water. This is an example of diffusion in (liquids/gases). When particles are 
(heated/cooled), they diffuse more quickly.

Resource sheet – Atoms and elements
An introduction to atomic structure
All matter is built from particles called atoms. Atoms are the building blocks of  
all materials on earth. More than 100 types of atoms have been discovered. We call  
them elements.
The structure of an atom
For a long time people thought that atoms were the smallest particles in existence.  
We now know that atoms are made up of even smaller sub-atomic particles: electrons, 
protons and neutrons.
•	 Electrons are very tiny and light. They have a negative charge.
•	 Protons are much larger and heavier than electrons and have a positive charge.
•	  Neutrons are larger and heavier like protons, but have no electrical charge (they are 
neutral).
How are the particles arranged?
An atom has a nucleus in its centre. Protons and neutrons can be found inside the 
nucleus. Electrons are constantly spinning around the outside of the nucleus. Each atom 
has an equal number of protons and electrons. This means it has no overall charge. 
Scientists use simple diagrams to show the structure of an atom. This is a diagram of a 
helium atom. It contains:
•	 2 protons
•	 2 neutrons
•	 2 electrons.

Refining crude oil
Crude oil is a fossil fuel that formed millions of years ago from buried dead plant 
and animal matter. These remains were turned into fossil fuels by heat and pressure. 
Crude oil is a mixture of different compounds. Most of the compounds in crude oil are 
hydrocarbons. The only atoms they contain are carbon and hydrogen.
Some common hydrocarbons found in crude oil
Chemical formula

Crude oil is separated into a number of different parts, called fractions, using a process 
called fractional distillation. This involves heating the crude oil until it evaporates and 
then letting the gas condense. The different hydrocarbons can be separated because 
they have different boiling points. The fractions are then processed into more useful 
hydrocarbons. Crude oil provides useful substances such as petrol, waxes, plastics, 
detergents, bitumen and man-made fibres such as nylon. 
The diagram shows the different substances formed from fractional distillation. 
Substances with a high boiling point condense at the bottom and substances with lower 
boiling points condense at the top.

Balancing chemical equations
You do not need to draw molecular diagrams each time to balance chemical equations. 
Look at the example below.
sodium chloride + fluorine gas 
 sodium fluoride + chlorine gas
 
NaCl 
+ 
F2 
 
NaF 
+ 
Cl2
At the start there is
1 atom Na + 1 atom Cl + 2 atoms F = 4 atoms in total
At the end there is
1 atom Na + 2 atoms Cl + 1 atom F = 4 atoms in total
Even though the total number of atoms is the same, the equation is not balanced because 
we have more atoms of fluorine and less of chlorine at the start of the reaction. We use 
trial and error to see what numbers we need to add to the front of the compounds.
 
2NaCl 
+ 
F2 
 
2NaF 
+ 
Cl2
If we put a 2 in front of the NaCl we now have 2 atoms of chlorine each side but now we 
have 2 atoms of sodium at the start of the reaction, so we also have to put a two at the 
front of NaF. Now there are two fluorine atoms on each side, so the equation is balanced.
Remember: A large number at the front means you multiply the number of atoms in 
one molecule by that number.

Resource sheet – Conservation of mass
Conserving mass (1)
When a chemical reaction occurs, the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to form the 
products. No new atoms are created, and none are destroyed. Mass is conserved. This 
means that the mass of the products at the end of the reaction is equal to the mass of the 
reactants at the beginning. We use molecular drawings to show this.
carbon C 
+ 
oxygen gas O2 
 
carbon dioxide CO2
 
 
 
 
The number of atoms of each element at the start is the same as at the end, so we say that 
the equation is balanced. What if the equation is not balanced?
magnesium Mg + 
oxygen gas O2 
 
magnesium oxide MgO
 
 
 
 
Something is wrong. There are more oxygen atoms at the start of the reaction than at the 
end, but we know that atoms cannot be lost during a chemical reaction. If there were two 
molecules of magnesium oxide at the end we would have the correct number of oxygen 
atoms, but one too many magnesium atoms. There must have been 2 magnesium atoms 
at the start of the reaction. 
 
 
+ 
 
 
 
2Mg 
 
+ 
O2 
 
 
2MgO
We say that this equation is balanced. We place a large number at the front to show how 
many molecules of each reactant and product there are. Placing a large number at the 
front of a formula multiplies the whole of the formula by that number. For example, 2MgO 
means 2 atoms of magnesium and 2 atoms of oxygen.

Resource sheet – Rates of reaction
Changing the rate of reaction (1) 
Chemical reactions take place at different speeds. Some reactions, 
such as explosions, take place very quickly, while others, like the 
rusting of a car, can take years. The rate of a reaction is a measure of 
how quickly a chemical reaction occurs. 
Reactions take place when particles collide with a certain amount of 
energy. Increasing the number of collisions and the energy that the particles collide with 
increases the rate of reaction. You can speed up or slow down a reaction by changing a 
number of different conditions.
1 Temperature
Increasing temperature speeds up the rate of reaction. As the temperature increases, the 
particles move faster and collide more often. This is why food is placed in fridges to slow 
down the chemical reactions that cause food to go off.
2 Concentration of solution
The concentration of a solution refers to the amount of a 
substance that is present in a certain amount of water. The more 
concentrated a solution is, the faster the reaction will occur, 
because there are more particles to collide into each other.
3 Size of particles
When a solid is crushed into smaller pieces there is more surface  
area in contact with the liquid. This means the particles collide 
with the liquid more often, speeding up the reaction.
4 Catalysts
Catalysts are substances that speed up 
the rate of reaction without being used 
up in the reaction. 
Less concentrated solution

comes from the acid used. For example, if calcium reacts with hydrochloric acid, the salt

Resource sheet – The periodic table
Naming groups in the periodic table
Elements on the periodic table can be divided into metals and non-metals. They can be 
further broken down into different groups based on their properties.
The metals found in Group 1 are very reactive. This means they react violently with 
water. They are also soft and can be cut with a knife. Examples include lithium, sodium 
and potassium, which are also known as the alkali metals. Hydrogen is in Group 1 of the 
periodic table but it is not considered part of the alkali metals because it is a non-metal.
The metals found between Groups 2 and 3 are called transition metals. They have the 
typical properties of metals – they are hard, dense and have high melting and boiling 
points. The semi-metals or metalloids are located along the stepped line between metals 
and non-metals. Boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium and polonium 
are all semi-metals. They are called semi-metals because they have some characteristics 
of metals and some of non-metals. For example, silicon is shiny, but it is brittle, so it would 
break it you hit it with a hammer.
The non-metals in Group 7 are very reactive. They are called halogens. Halogens are 
poisonous non-metals. Examples include fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. 
Like most non-metals, they have low melting and boiling points. 
Group 8 – sometimes known as Group 0 – is found on the right-hand side of the periodic 
table. These elements are very special because they do not react to form compounds. They 
are found by themselves in nature. They are called noble gases.

Resource sheet – The periodic table
How is the periodic table arranged?
The periodic table is arranged like a grid. The elements appear in order of increasing 
atomic mass and are placed in a specific location because of the way they look and act.
Rows
•	 The elements are placed in rows. All horizontal rows are called periods.
•	 All elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells. 
•	 There are seven periods, but elements 57–71 and 89–103 have been placed underneath 
to make the table a more manageable shape.
Columns
•	 Elements are arranged in vertical columns called groups (1–8), with the transition 
metals between groups 2 and 3. For example, group 1 consists of H, Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr.
•	 The transition metals in the centre section behave a bit differently, so are not included. 
•	 All elements except hydrogen in group 1 share similar properties. Hydrogen is a special 
element, so is often placed above group 1.
•	 The group number also represents the number of electrons in the outer shell. This 
number affects how reactive the element is. The most reactive elements have very few 
electrons in their outer shell, or only need a few more to fill it.

Drought and Australian ecosystems 
Drought describes a time of abnormally low rainfall in a certain area, when there is not 
enough water to meet normal needs. Australia is often affected by drought. Sometimes a 
drought can last for many years. 
If water supplies in an ecosystem are low for a long time, plants wither and die. This 
causes food shortages for all the living things that rely on those plants for food, and loss 
of shelter for some animals. Eventually, the animals that do not have enough food stop 
breeding and may die out. The food web of an ecosystem can be harmed in this way. In 
places where drought has gone on for a long time, some ecosystems never recover.

How do animals in ecosystems 
compete for food?
All animals need to eat food. Plant-eaters may forage (search) for food among the plants, 
picking fruits, berries and nuts from trees and bushes. Others graze on crops planted by 
humans or grass. Most meat-eaters hunt and kill other animals. 
Sometimes animals need to get their share of food by fighting each other. This is  
called competition. Sometimes it might be two members of the same species that are 
fighting – for example, two young monkeys might fight over a piece of fruit. Sometimes it 
is two different kinds of animals that fight for food – for example, a hyena might try to take 
some food from a lion.

Achieve!
Relationships
Living things in an ecosystem interact in different ways. Some living things have learned 
to depend on each other to survive. 
Collaboration
Animals of the same species may live in groups, rather than on their own. A group of 
animals from the same species is called a population. As a population, animals can share 
the jobs of finding food and water, protecting each other from predators, raising their 
young and finding shelter. This is called collaboration. It means ‘working together’. 
Symbiotic relationships
Certain species develop a relationship with a completely different species that benefits 
one or both animals. This is called a symbiotic relationship. When the symbiotic 
relationship benefits both species it is called mutualism. An example is the clownfish, 
which lives amongst the poisonous tentacles of a sea anemone. The clownfish protects 
the anemone from the bigger fish that eat anemones. In return, the clownfish is protected 
from predators by the anemone’s stinging tentacles. The clownfish is not hurt because it 
has a special mucus on its skin that protects it from the sting.

26

Food chains
In an ecosystem, one organism depends on another to survive. Producers make food, 
which is then eaten by consumers, which is then broken down by decomposers. 
Consumers and decomposers turn this food into the energy they need to survive. This 
creates what scientists call a food chain. 
A food chain can be represented using pictures or words, but it always needs arrows. 
The arrows show what is eaten by what and the flow of energy along the food chain. 
They point away from the thing that is being eaten. For example:
plant ➝ grasshopper ➝ snake ➝ eagle
Sometimes food chains show decomposers. Sometimes they show just producers and 
consumers, or just consumers.

been done for you. Hint: Make sure your organisms are in the correct order.  The  
correct order may not be the order in which they appear in the statement. Check 
your answers by replacing each arrow in the food chain with ‘is eaten by’.
a) A scorpion is eaten by a meerkat, which is eaten by a cobra, which is eaten by a 
vulture.
 
scorpion ➝ meerkat ➝ cobra ➝ vulture
b) A tiger eats a deer, which eats a plant. 
 
plant ➝ deer ➝ tiger
c) A ferret eats a rabbit, which eats grass.
 
 
d) A brown bear eats a salmon, which eats plankton.

Food webs
Instead of drawing or writing a food chain, we can better show the many relationships 
between living things in an ecosystem by drawing a food web. 
There is often more than one species that eats another in an ecosystem. Food webs are 
used to describe the diets of animals that have a variety of food sources, and they are also 
used to show all the relationships between creatures in a particular ecosystem.

Producers, consumers and decomposers
All the organisms in an ecosystem can be grouped into one of three types, depending on 
what they eat. 
 
●Producers are living things that make (or produce) their own food from inorganic 
(non-living) ingredients. Examples of producers are green plants.
 
●Consumers are organisms that cannot make their own food. They either eat or 
use food products made by producers or other living things that eat producers. 
Examples of consumers are insects and snakes.
 
●Decomposers break down organic matter (dead plants and animals) by making it 
rot or decay, releasing nutrients, and then absorb the nutrients as food. Examples 
of decomposers are bacteria and fungi. Many decomposers are microscopic 
organisms, called microorganisms.

What is a consumer?
Consumers are types of organisms that eat or use food products made by producers or 
that eat other consumers. Large land mammals, birds and reptiles are consumers.
There are three main types of consumers:
 
●herbivores (consumers that eat plants)
 
●carnivores (consumers that eat animals, or meat) 
 
●omnivores (consumers that eat both plants and animals). 
Humans are omnivores. We eat all sorts of foods produced by plants, and we also eat 
other animals that eat plants and animals.

What is a decomposer?
A decomposer is a living thing that works to break down organic materials into smaller 
parts. For example, a decomposer breaks down fruit on a forest floor by making it rot or 
decay. The decomposer absorbs the nutrients from the remains and also releases some 
nutrients into the soil. 
Fungi and moulds are decomposers. They decompose plant waste, including 
vegetables. Some small organisms from the animal kingdom are also decomposers, 
including worms, slugs, millipedes and termites, which break down logs and sticks. Other 
decomposers, like maggots and flies, help to break down dead animal carcasses (bodies). 
Dung (animal droppings) is broken down by dung flies and beetles. Microorganisms, 
including various bacteria, break down all kinds of substances, including milk, eggs and 
meat products.

balance. Food chains and food webs can be affected in ways that threaten the survival of

BACKGROUND
mammals (say ‘ma-mels’) – warm-blooded animals with backbones that feed their young with milk
Humans are an important part of the biodiversity of ecosystems.
Human reproduction
Humans reproduce in the same way as other mammals. After sexual intercourse, a single 
sperm cell fertilises the female’s ovum (egg). Usually, one egg is released from the 
female’s ovaries every month. If the male sperm cell reaches the egg at just the right time, 
the sperm goes into the egg and the two cells join together and begin multiplying. The 
cells continue to grow for nine months inside the female’s womb. The human baby is born 
after passing through the female’s vagina (birth canal).

called sexual (intercourse / joining).
d) An egg has been fertilised if a (sperm cell / ovum) has gone into it.
e) The multiplying cells eventually become an (embryo / womb).
f) The baby travels through the (ovaries / vagina) during birth.

Changing behaviour
Adaptation is the name that scientists give to the way that living things change and 
become better suited to their habitats. They also use the word adaptation to describe the 
actual change. 
Adaptations may be behavioural or physical. Physical adaptations in species happen 
over many generations, but a species can change its behaviour more easily. This is called 
behavioural adaptation.
+ 1  What word do we use to describe the way that some organisms go through 
changes that help them become better suited to their environment?
 
 
2 What smaller (root) word can be found in this term? a     p  
3 What does the word in Question 2 mean? Circle one answer:

Many organisms can make outward changes to suit their environment. For example,  
long-haired dogs such as Siberian huskies are able to keep warm in cold habitats because 
of their thick coats. When a dog like this is placed in a warmer habitat it must change its 
behaviour so it can cope with the different temperature. It changes its behaviour, so this is 
behavioural adaptation.

Competition in ecosystems
Ecosystems do not always operate in peace and harmony. The living things in an 
ecosystem have different needs, which cause them to compete in a number of ways. 
Animals compete for food, water and shelter in order to survive. They also compete 
amongst members of their own species for mating partners and they fight to protect  
their offspring. 
Even plants compete in order to survive. Plants produce their own food by using 
sunlight and other ingredients to make sugars. In an area crowded with plants, they must 
compete with the other plants for sunlight – for example, rainforest plants grow taller and 
taller so they can rise above the rainforest canopy (roof of leaves) and reach the sunlight. 
Plants must compete for growing space, water and nutrients in the soil. They also compete 
to attract insects that help them to reproduce.

Relationships in ecosystems
There are many types of relationships between living things in an ecosystem. Some 
relationships place two living things against each other (for example, the relationship 
between an animal that hunts and eats another animal). Other relationships can benefit 
one or both organisms. 
Mutualism is a type of relationship between different living things that benefits both. For 
example, a small fish that eats a special type of algae lives amongst a group of bigger fish 
that have this algae growing on their skin. The smaller fish cleans up the skin of the bigger 
fish by nibbling at the algae. Both types of fish benefit. The little fish gets fed, and the 
bigger fish gets rid of its skin problem.

Activity sheet – Living things and ecosystems
What is an ecosystem?
An ecosystem is a complex system that includes all the plants, animals and non-living 
things found in a certain place, as well as all the different ways those things interact.  
We say that something interacts with something else when it acts in a way that affects  
the other thing. 
For example, a garden pond contains living things – also called organisms – such as 
frogs, snails, fish, water birds, water plants and algae, as well as non-living things such as 
fresh water, rocks, sand, air, sunlight and soil. The garden pond ecosystem is all of these 
living and non-living things as well as all of the ways these things interact and depend on 
each other – from a fish eating a snail to water lilies using sunlight to make food. All the 
living things in an ecosystem are known as a community. The variety of living things in 
the ecosystem is known as the ecosystem’s biodiversity.

What is a habitat?
BACKGROUND
species (say ‘spee-seas’) – a group of living things that can breed together to produce fertile offspring
The particular place where a population of a living thing lives is called its habitat.  
A population is a group of animals from the same species that lives in the same space, 
such as a population of gorillas in a mountain range. A habitat can be as big as a rainforest 
or as small as a burrow, depending on how much space the population needs. 
Many living things need to be able to find food, water, clean air, shelter, warmth, light 
and safety in their environment. When one or more of these basic needs is no longer 
available – for example, if drinking water is no longer available in drier months – the 
population may sometimes move to a new habitat.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Ecosystems
53
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Activity sheet – Plant and animal biodiversity 
Adaptation
Adaptation is the name that scientists give to the way that living things change and 
become better suited to their habitats. 
Offspring are not identical to either of their parents. Each new generation of a species 
is a tiny bit different from the one before. The theory of evolution says that these tiny 
differences are not noticeable from generation to generation, but over thousands or 
millions of years these small differences can completely and obviously change the way a 
plant or animal looks or functions. Adaptation results in new species and new subspecies. 
In this way it contributes to the biodiversity, or biological diversity, of life on Earth.
+ 1 Explain why you think offspring are not identical to either of their parents.
 
 
 
 
The process of adaptation happens because of small variations within a species. 
Variations that give some individuals a better chance of survival than other individuals in 
their species lead to what we call ‘survival of the fittest’, or natural selection. An example 
of a variation that might give a better chance of survival is a different fur colour, which 
might make it easier for a small animal to hide from predators.
Because the changed individuals are more likely to survive, they are more likely to 
breed and produce offspring. Their offspring are more likely to have the changed feature, 
or trait. Over time, this can result in a complete change to all the individuals in a species. 
The new species trait is called the adaptive trait, or the adaptation.

DNA, chromosomes and genes
A new life begins as just one cell. All the information for growing a living thing is found 
inside the nucleus of this cell. For most animals, this cell is a fertilised egg, containing 
genetic information from two parents. This genetic information is stored in DNA, in 
genes and chromosomes.
DNA
 
●The letters DNA stand for deoxyribonucleic acid (say de-ox-ee-rye-bo-new-clee-ick 
ass-id). When people talk about DNA, they usually mean the information that DNA 
contains, not the acid itself. 
 
●DNA is found inside the cells of nearly all living things. 
 
●DNA is like a set of instructions for building and operating a living thing. It provides 
the information to make the proteins that make up cells, as well as instructions as 
to how the cells form, what shape they will be, what things they can do and so on. 
Chromosomes and genes
 
●Chromosomes are tiny threads made of DNA. Genes are short pieces of these 
threads. 
 
●Each chromosome consists of thousands of different genes. 
 
●Every gene carries information about a specific characteristic. 
 
●Chromosomes are found inside the nucleus of cells. In each cell, the genetic 
information is exactly the same, containing the same instructions. 
 
●Chromosomes come in pairs. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. 
 
●One chromosome of every pair comes from the mother and one in every pair 
comes from the father.

How do animals reproduce?
Animals come in all shapes and sizes. Most of them reproduce through sexual 
reproduction, but they breed and have their young in many different ways.
Two partners
Sexual reproduction requires two partners of the opposite sex. Because of this, all species 
that reproduce sexually come in two different forms: males and females. An important 
principle of sexual reproduction is that the male and female must be of the same species 
if they are to successfully reproduce.
In some species, males and females look very different. In other species, the differences 
are not so obvious.

Activity sheet – Plant and animal biodiversity 
How do plants reproduce?
All plants and animals reproduce. Reproduction may be asexual (without sex) or sexual. 
A plant that reproduces asexually produces a new plant by itself. The new plant is 
genetically identical to the parent plant. This is because it has the same genes as the 
parent plant. Genes are information carried in a living thing’s cells that determines some 
of its characteristics.
A plant that reproduces sexually produces a new plant through fertilisation, either 
by itself or with another plant. The new plant is genetically different to both the parent 
plants, because it has a combination of the genes of its parents.

Pollination
Flowering plants reproduce through a process called pollination. Flowers contain the 
reproductive organs of a plant. Some plants have flowers with both male and female parts, 
while other plants have flowers with only male parts or only female parts.

Natural selection
Natural selection is the term we give to the way in which a particular animal or plant 
survives to breed. Natural selection results in species adaptation. Evolutionary scientists 
call this process evolution by natural selection.
Some animals within a species – a group of rabbits, for example – will be healthier, 
stronger and quicker than others. If this group of rabbits were to be chased by a wolf 
or a fox, the ‘fittest’ ones would survive to breed because they could run faster and for 
longer periods of time. These better-adapted rabbits would eventually have babies, and 
most of the young rabbits might also inherit their parents’ strength and fitness. Over 
time, the less fit rabbits would die out and the stronger, fitter, faster rabbits would survive. 
Nature is ‘selecting’ those rabbits to be the ones that pass their genes down to a new 
generation.

Bushfires and Australian ecosystems
Australia is a very hot and dry country. In the summer months, bushfires threaten natural 
habitats all over Australia. Sometimes bushfires start because of lightning strikes or other 
natural processes. Other times they are deliberately lit and controlled by authorities. 
Indigenous Australians used controlled burns for thousands of years before Europeans 
came to Australia. 
Although fire destroys some plants in an ecosystem, it encourages other plants to grow. 
Fire heats up the seed pods of certain trees and plants, such as the banksia plant. When 
the pressure inside the pod builds up, it bursts open and releases its seeds, which begins  
a new crop of trees. 
Some animals in an ecosystem benefit from bushfires too. Fire encourages new plants 
to grow and it can reduce animal numbers, which means there is more food and less 
competition for the surviving animals. Fire also clears old vegetation (plant growth), 
creating new habitats and shelters for animals.

Achieve!
Floods and Australian ecosystems
Flooding occurs in Australian ecosystems when land that is normally dry becomes 
covered in water. When there is heavy rain, rivers and creeks may fill up and burst their 
banks, covering the surrounding land in water. At some times of the year, there may be 
little rainfall in an area and the ground becomes very hard and dry. When heavy summer 
rains come, lots of water can fall very quickly. This leads to run-off, where water travels 
across the ground too quickly to be soaked into the soil. A lot of run-off can cause a fast-
moving flood, called a flash flood. 
Floods can be very damaging to some parts of ecosystems. Habitats may be destroyed 
and animals may drown, upsetting the delicate balance of the ecosystem. But some 
species benefit from flooding. River red gums need flooding for their seeds to germinate 
(sprout), and populations of frogs, fish and wetland birds can grow in number after floods.

Activity sheet – Plants in ecosystems 
How do plants compete for food?
Living things compete for food in a number of ways. Plants make their food by using 
sunlight, water and other ingredients to make sugars that help them grow. In areas that 
are crowded with plants, they must compete with other plants for sunlight and water. 
Rainforest trees that have their leaves at the top of the canopy (the rainforest ‘roof’) get 
the most sunlight. The plants that are lower down get less sunlight, so they are not able to 
grow as easily, which is why they stay shorter.

Photosynthesis and ecosystems
Green plants produce their own food using photosynthesis. This food helps them grow.  
As the plant grows, more leaves, fruit and flowers are made available for other living  
things to eat. In this way, photosynthesis helps an ecosystem to thrive. 
Plants use carbon dioxide, water and the sun’s energy to make a sugary food called 
glucose. When the plant is eaten by a consumer, some of the energy stored in the glucose 
is released and used by the consumer. The rest of the energy is released as heat. When 
consumers and producers die, decomposers break down their remains into tiny parts 
called nutrients. These nutrients go into the soil or the atmosphere. A new plant uses 
these nutrients to begin the energy transfer process all over again.

Achieve!
The importance of plants in ecosystems
Plants are a very important part of ecosystems for a number of reasons. One reason is that 
they are producers, which means they make their own food from inorganic (non-living) 
ingredients, and other living things consume this food. Another important reason is that 
as they are making food they take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. 
Green plants take in carbon dioxide gas through their leaves. Carbon dioxide, 
water and sunlight are used during a process called photosynthesis to help the plant 
produce a sugary food called glucose. When the plant breaks down water during 
photosynthesis, one of the waste products is oxygen. The plant releases the oxygen 
through its leaves. Most animals, including humans, need oxygen in the air they 
breathe for respiration.
The word equation for photosynthesis is:  
carbon dioxide + water (+ light energy) = glucose + oxygen
The chemical formula for carbon dioxide gas is CO2 (one part carbon and two 
parts oxygen).
The chemical formula for water is H2O (two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen).

The importance of blood 
+ 1 Read the following information about blood and then answer the questions.
All animals, including humans, need certain things if they are to stay healthy and 
survive. Some things that are vital to life are water, oxygen, nutrients from food and a 
way of getting rid of waste products. All animals must have a way of transporting water, 
oxygen, nutrients and waste products around the body, to and from every single cell. In 
vertebrates (animals with a backbone), these substances are carried in the bloodstream.
Blood is made up of red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets travelling around 
the body in a fluid called plasma.

The network of vessels that carry blood is called the circulatory system. When blood 
travels around the body, we call it circulation. The heart is the organ that pumps the blood 
around the circulatory system.

How do we know about cells?
Cells are tiny parcels of matter that can’t be seen with the 
naked eye. Before people knew about tiny, invisible things 
such as cells, bacteria (or germs) and viruses, they believed 
that bad spirits caused diseases. 
Over the years, different kinds of microscopes have been 
invented. In the late 1600s scientists began to see cells for 
the first time. Scientists today use powerful microscopes to 
find out more about cells, such as what different cells do and 
how they work. This has helped us to treat illnesses and show 
people how to stay healthy.

would have happened.
a) Robert Hooke first discovers the cell.  
b) Zacharias Janssen invents the compound microscope.  
c) Theodor Schwann and Matthias Schleiden state that plants and animals are made 
up of cells.  
2 a)  Microscopic is a synonym of tiny. What is the base word of microscopic? Hint: It is 
mentioned in this Activity sheet.

Reproduction
All types of living things are able to produce ‘offspring’ (descendants) that are almost 
copies of themselves. This process is called reproduction. Reproductive systems enable 
living things to make seeds, lay eggs, have babies or produce offspring in other ways.
+ 1 Read the following passage and then write short answers to the following 
questions.
 
In humans, there are two sexes: males and females. Both carry genetic material called 
DNA in their cells. When one cell from each partner combine, the DNA of the two 
parents mixes together. The male provides the sperm cell and the female provides 
the egg cell. The sperm fertilises the egg, entering through the cell membrane and 
releasing its contents. In this way, the two cells combine. The new cell begins to divide. 
It grows and develops into a new human.

Activity sheet – Body systems and cells
Tissues, organs and body systems
Similar types of cells group together in an animal’s body to form a tissue, such as a muscle, 
which carries out a particular job. Different tissues group together to form an organ. 
An organ is a complete unit of the body that has a particular role or job to do. For example, 
the human heart is a fist-sized organ made up of cardiac muscle and connective tissues. 
Its function is to pump blood around the body.
Two or more organs work together in groups called body systems.
There are body systems for all sorts of things – including for breathing, for moving 
blood around the body and for digesting food. All the cells in a system need to do their 
jobs to make the whole system work.

Animal cells
Most types of animal cells have a centre called a nucleus near their middle, which is 
surrounded by a jelly-like substance called cytoplasm. Around this is the cell membrane. 
Cells also contain things called proteins and organelles. Proteins are a special kind of 
nutrient that are an essential part of all living things. Organelles are tiny, living machines 
that are found inside cells. The organelles perform various jobs to keep the cell alive. Types 
of organelles include: 
 
●mitochondria, which provide energy for the cell to use
 
●ribosomes, which are like protein factories
 
●vacuoles, which are water-filled organelles that can have many functions
 
●Golgi bodies, which process proteins.

Cell division
Cells do not last forever. They grow old and eventually die, so they need to be replaced. 
For example, skin cells in humans get worn out and are replaced continually. The flaky bits 
of dry skin that you scrub away are made of dead skin cells. Underneath this skin, healthy 
new skin cells are ready to replace the lost cells.
Cells also make living things grow bigger or stronger, by producing more of 
themselves. For example, a plant grows taller and gets more leaves as new cells are made.
To make more of themselves, cells separate into two parts that are the same. This is 
called cell division. Its scientific name is mitosis.

old cells and (kill / create) new cells for growth. This process is called mitosis. Through 
mitosis, a (cell / plant) splits into (three / two), creating an (identical / adult) copy of

Plant cells
Like animal cells, most plant cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane. Plant cells 
also have a hard cell wall made of cellulose. Also like animal cells, plant cells contain tiny, 
living machines called organelles. Golgi bodies and ribosomes are two organelles found 
in plant cells. They have special jobs to do in the cell to help the plant grow and to keep it 
healthy. Plant cells also contain large water-filled containers called vacuoles.
Green plants contain important organelles called chloroplasts. These parts have a 
chemical called chlorophyll in them. It is green. Green plants get their green colour from 
the chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are involved in the way that green plants use sunlight to 
produce food, through photosynthesis.

All living things are made up of tiny parcels of matter called cells. Cells are the  
smallest units of living things. This is why they are sometimes called the building  
blocks of life. 
Living things may be made up of just one cell or many billions of cells. Anything that is 
made up of one or more cells is considered a form of life or lifeform.
The bodies of all types of animals, including humans, are made up of cells. Different 
types of cells have different functions or jobs. Human bodies are made up of hundreds of 
different types of cells, including types of blood cells, nerve cells and skin cells. 
All types of plants are made up of cells, too. Plant cells and animal cells have some 
similar parts and some different parts.

Genus and species
We classify living things in groups because they are alike (similar) or unalike (different). 
Similarities may include the way something moves, what it looks like or how it reproduces. 
However, animals and plants with the same characteristics or features are only grouped 
together as a species if they are related genetically. For example, two butterflies may look 
very much alike, but they may not be closely related. Members of the same species can 
breed together to produce fertile offspring; if they can’t, they are not considered part of 
the same species.
Writing scientific names
When we write a living thing’s scientific name, we include the genus and the species. The 
genus is the first part of the name and begins with a capital letter and appears in italics. 
The species comes second and is written in lower case letters and italics.

Other ways of grouping organisms
There are all sorts of features that can help us organise groups of living things. Organisms 
can be grouped by biological classification, but they can also be grouped by where 
they live (habitat), what they eat or how they behave. For example, the blue-billed duck 
(Oxyura australis) is grouped with other birds in the Class Aves (Birds), but it could also be 
grouped with Australian wetland creatures. 
Many different types of organisms can live together in the same habitat. Some 
organisms that share the same living area depend on each other for their survival. For 
example, organisms that live on coral reefs are interdependent, which means that they 
all need each other to survive. Some organisms are food for others, while some provide 
shelter or protection to other species.
+ 1 Read the passage and underline all the plants and animals mentioned.
 
A coral reef is home to many different types of life. Reefs contain lots of different 
species of fish. These fish eat the seaweed and grasses that grow on the coral. It 
is important that there is a rich supply of food for all the reef’s creatures. Sharks 
and other predators eat large fish, which in turn eat smaller fish. All sorts of plants 
and animals live in tropical reef habitats. They include eels, crabs, prawns, sea stars, 
seahorses, plankton, seaweed, anemones, clownfish, angelfish, coral polyps, sea turtles, 
jellyfish, dolphins, dugongs and whales.

ACHIEVE!   Science – Living things
29
© Ally Chumley and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
The hierarchy of biological 
classification
The biological classification system has seven ranks or levels. The groups in the higher 
levels are larger and broader. They group living things that have just some things in 
common. The groups in the lower levels are smaller and more specific. They group living 
things that have many more things in common. The organisation of these groups is called 
the hierarchy of classification. Scientists sometimes disagree with the way others group 
organisms. For example, some scientists use only five kingdoms.
Level
Kingdom
There are six kingdoms in the classification system: animal, plant, protista 
(single-celled organisms including amoebae), fungi, bacteria, archaebacteria 
(microorganisms also called extremophiles).
Phylum
There are more than 30 phyla in the Animal Kingdom and 10 in the Plant Kingdom. 
For example, Phylum Chordata includes humans, birds, fish and all other animals 
with a backbone. 
Class
Each phylum is divided into classes. For example, Phylum Chordata includes the 
classes of amphibians, birds, mammals, reptiles and fish.
Order
An order is a subcategory of a class. 
Family
Families are smaller groups within orders.
Genus
Species that share certain characteristics may be closely related, so they are 
grouped together in a genus. 
Species
A species is a group of living things that can breed to produce fertile offspring.

Body systems working together
The human body contains a number of important organs. Each organ is made up of 
millions of cells that have very specialised functions. For example, the heart is an organ 
that pumps blood around the body. Heart cells function quite differently from the cells 
of other organs, such as lung cells. Lung cells have special parts that help them collect 
oxygen for red blood cells. Lungs enable humans to breathe air in and provide the oxygen 
that cells need to survive. In the central nervous system, nerve cells send electric signals 
to another important organ – the brain. Brain cells are very delicate and control other 
systems in the body. The spinal cord is part of the system that involves electrical signals 
being passed to and from the brain.

What else are bodies made of? 
Animals and humans are made of cells, which make up tissues, which make up organs, 
which work together in groups to make up body systems. The bodies of humans and 
some other animals are built around a structure called a skeleton. We call all the bones 
and joints in the body the skeletal system. The bones of our bodies help us stay upright 
and give us proper shape and strength. Plants do not need skeletons because they have 
hard cell walls, which give their tissues a solid frame. 
Attached to the human skeleton are muscles. Muscles allow us to move. Muscles are 
attached to bones by tissues called tendons. Muscles work together to push and pull on 
our bones, giving us the ability to move. When a muscle pulls, we say it contracts. When 
the muscle stops pulling, we say it is relaxed. Bones are joined together at places in the 
body called joints. Knees and elbows are examples of joints. Inside our joints, strings called 
ligaments tie the bones together.

How do plants get food?
Just like animals, plants need food to produce energy, so they can grow and survive. Plants 
have two main types of food: organic and inorganic. Organic means coming from living 
things, and inorganic means coming from things that are not living.
Inorganic foods are the minerals that plants get from the earth. They are nutrients that 
are found in the soil that the plants grow in. Minerals in the soil are dissolved in water and 
sucked up (absorbed) by the plant’s roots. In areas where the soil is poor quality – either 
with too few nutrients or too many of one kind of nutrient – humans can add fertilisers to 
give plants more inorganic nutrients. 
Green plants can also make their own organic food, using sunlight and two important 
inorganic nutrients: carbon dioxide and water. The name for the organic food that plants 
make out of inorganic nutrients is glucose. The process of making glucose is called 
photosynthesis.

Photosynthesis
Photosynthesis is the name we give to a special process that green plants use to make 
food using sunlight, or light energy. They use light energy to change carbon dioxide and 
water into a special sugar called glucose. Plants get their energy from glucose, and this 
energy allows them to grow and carry out all sorts of functions. 
Green plant cells contain a green chemical called chlorophyll, which traps light energy 
from the sun. During photosynthesis, water molecules are split apart using this light 
energy. The hydrogen parts of each water molecule join with carbon dioxide to make 
glucose, the special sugar that plants have as their food. The leftover oxygen part of each 
water molecule is released by the plant through its leaves.
The word photosynthesis is made up of two parts – photo means ‘light’ and synthesis 
means ‘to make something’.

Plant structures
Most green plants have some common structures. These structures play different parts in 
the process of making food (photosynthesis) and distributing this food around the plant.
In most flowering plants, there are roots below the ground. They keep the plant in place 
by holding on to the soil. Roots absorb water for the plant to use in photosynthesis. 
Cells in the plant’s leaves carry out the work of photosynthesis, creating food (glucose) 
by absorbing sunlight and using water and carbon dioxide.
Many flowering plants have a system of tubes inside their stems. Two of these tubes are 
called the xylem and the phloem. 
 
●The xylem carries water from the plant’s roots around to all the plant’s cells. 
 
●The phloem carries food (glucose) from the leaves to the rest of the plant. This gives 
each cell the energy it needs to survive and grow.

BOOK 1; CHARACTERISTICS OF LIVING THINGS

The discovery of the cell

The first cell ever observed and illustrated was the empty, dead shell of a once living plant. In 1665 the English
scientist Robert Hooke (1635-1703) used a reasonably new invention, the microscope, to look closely at a thinly
sliced piece of cork. The empty ‘shell’ of what was once living plant matter brought to mind tiny rooms called
cells (from the Latin, cellula, meaning ‘small compartment’). Some books state that Hooke named them after
the celis of monasteries, while others cite the cells of honeycombs, but whatever inspired him, Hooke named
them well.

It took another 170 years before the living contents of cells were discovered, Bohemian physiologist Johannes
von Purkinje (1787-1869) recognised that cells had to be composed of a living matter since they formed a
part of living matter.* He named the matter protoplasm (proto first, plasm form). French scientist Felix
Dujardin (1801-1860) eventually observed the protoplasm. Dujardin called it sarcode, from the Greek sarkos,
meaning ‘flesh’.

* Matthias Schieiden (1804-1881) confirmed this for plants in 1838.

Not long after Dujardin observed the protoplasm, German scientist Theodor Schwann (1810-1882) made the
first really detailed inspection of animal cells. It soon became clear that both plants and animals possess cells,
each with structures that were unique to the group and many that were common to both. It was Schwann who
showed us that every tissue of every organism is made of cells. Prior to this many people recognised that cells
formed a part of an organism, but they did not realise that every structure could be reduced to cellular
components. It was then understood that the husk-like walls, which formed the once living cells of the tree, had
created the cork.

The history of microscopy

Ever since humans have studied the world around them, people have wanted to see things with greater detail
than the naked eye permitted. An important event that advanced the development of cell theory was the
invention of the microscope. There is some debate about specific dates and relative importance of contributions,
but the following all played a part.

In Holland, near the end of the sixteenth century, both Hans Lippershey and the father and son team of

Hans and Zacharias Janssen were credited with the invention of microscopes. Dutch clockmaker Anton van
Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723) was also recognised with inventing the first practical microscope-like instrument.
Leeuwenhoek’s device was just two lenses which, he discovered by accident, dramatically increased magnification
when placed one over the other, Robert Hooke (1635-1703) built another important microscope, Hooke’s
reflecting microscope was described in his 1665 book Micrographia, along with his illustrations of many of

the objects he examined using it.

A microscope with two or more lenses in it is a compound microscope (compound to combine or put together).
The word fens comes from the Latin word for lentil, which is the shape of a convex lens.

Marcello Malpighi (1628-1694) was an Italian physiologist who, in 1661, used a microscope to study blood
circulation. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden, a German botanist, studied plant parts under a microscope and
discovered that plant parts are made of cells. A year later, Theodor Schwann, a German zoologist, examined
animal parts under a microscope and revealed that animal parts are also made of cells.

Around 1880 to 1890 Pasteur and Koch made many discoveries using microscopes. Louis Pasteur (1822-1896)
used the microscope for his work on yeast and bacteria while, in 1876, Robert Koch discovered the microbes

Classification III: Invertebrates

Invertebrates are animals without internal backbones. They are usually less complex than vertebrates. There are
over a million species of invertebrates. We can subdivide invertebrates into smaller groups depending on their
characteristics. The groups we use are echinoderms, coelenterates, flatworms, segmented worms, molluscs and
arthropods,

Echinoderms all live in the sea. They have a spiny skin. Starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers are all echinoderms.

Coelenterates nearly all live in the sea. They often have stinging cells. Jellyfish,
hydra and sea anemones and coral are all coelenterates.

Flatworms are very simple creatures. They live in water or as parasites (live on
other creatures), They all have flat bodies. Liver flukes, tapeworms and planaria
are flatworms,

Segmented worms have long, thin and rounded bodies divided into segments
(parts). Earthworms and leeches are segmented worms.

Molluscs mostly live in the sea or fresh water. They usually have shells. Many
have a large ‘foot’, Snails, octopuses, clams and oysters are molluscs.

Arthropods all have an exoskeleton (strong outside case). This is the largest group
in the animal kingdom. Arthropod bodies are in sections and their legs are in pairs and jointed.
Because it is such a large group, it is further divided into insects, arachnids, myriapods and crustaceans.

Insects have six legs. Their bodies are in three parts. Many insects have wings. The bee, housefly and ant are
all insects.

Arachnids have eight legs and their bodies are divided into two parts. There are over 60 000 species of
arachnids. As well as spiders this class includes scorpions, mites and ticks.

All reptiles, even those that live in water, breathe through their lungs. Most are oviparous (lay eqqs) but some are

warm ground. They are usually found in warmer regions of the Earth. In temperate regions they tend to hibernate
in colder weather, and in very hot conditions they estivate (go into a torpor). Reptiles have been on Earth for
around 300 million years.

Ectotherms and endotherms

Multicellutar animals can only survive within a relatively narrow band of temperatures. lan
There are exceptions but the lower limit is usually 0°C (freezing point of water) and 45°C
(when proteins are denatured, or ‘cooked'). The optimum temperatures for particular
organisms are even more restricted.

1 Explain what is meant by optimum temperature.

Cellular respiration releases energy when glucose is oxidised (combines with oxygen to
form carbon dioxide and water). Most of this energy is released as heat and will affect the
body temperature of the organism. We can divide animals into two groups, depending on
how their body temperature is requlated ~ ectotherms and endotherms.

Ectotherms

Many animals lose most of the heat energy generated from cellular respiration to their
environment. Their body temperature is variable and is determined by their surroundings.
These animals are ectotherms. You may also see such animals referred to as being
poikilothermic (having variable temperatures) or even (inaccurately) as being cold-
blooded. Usually their body temperature is only slightly higher than ambient temperature
but, depending on their activity level, can be much warmer than their surroundings.

2 Explain what is meant by ambient temperature.

Animals can absorb heat from the sun or hot surfaces (generally heated by the sun), They
lose heat by radiation from their bodies, evaporation (perspiration etc) and conduction to
cold surfaces. Water conducts heat better than air does, but large masses of water vary less
in temperature than the atmosphere. This is because water has a greater heat capacity
than air and takes longer to heat up and cool down, Aquatic ectotherms are well adapted
to the temperature of their surroundings. Terrestrial ectotherms need to have greater

responses to extremes of temperature. 8

Human systems |

Humans (and other animals) have specialised structures to obtain nutrients from their environment.
These structures are made up of many components.

1 Arrange the following in terms of increasing complexity:
organs, atoms, cells, tissues, organism, molecule, organ system

Human systems involved in the maintenance of life include those dealing with circulation, respiration, excretion,
nerves and glands.

The circulatory system

The circulatory (or vascular) system Is a closed —- Cross section of blood vessels

network of blood-filled tubes, or blood vessets.

Blood: Is. kept flowing one way through these Artery Vein Capillary
vessels by the pumping of the heart. The heart is
a muscle with four compartments. The upper oO
two compartments are called atria and the lower
compartments are ventrices. An adult human
has about 5.5 litres of blood in circulation. Blood
distributes heat and many important materials
‘throughout the body. How often a heart beats
(contracts) is called the pulse rate.

There are three main types of blood vessels: arteries, veins and capillaries.

2 Study the diagrams of blood vessels. Compare the relative quantity of blood each is likely to be able to carry.
Explain how you reached your conclusion.

Arteries are wide, thick-walled vessels which carry blood away from the heart, Arterioles are smaller arteries
that branch from larger arteries. All arteries (apart from those going to the lungs) contain dissolved oxygen and
are bright red in colour. All arteries also carry blood that contains dissolved food and waste products. The food
reaches body cells by means of the capillaries. Non-gas waste products are taken to the kidneys where they are
Processed and eventually passed out of the body as urine.

Capillaries are narrow, thin-walled vessels between 0,13 mm to 0.20 mm in diameter. They branch off from
arterioles and then rejoin to form veins. Capillaries connected to the digestive system pick up dissolved food.
