BOOK 2: GENETICS

Genetic issues in the 21st century

Many of you will be familiar with the term genethics, or the ethics (morals) behind genetic research, Since 2001,
a few new terms have arisen, two of which you will probably hear at some time. These are genomics, a word
that refers to an organism's genome (complete genetic make-up) and proteomics, which refers to the complete
set of proteins found within an organism ~ and there are many!

It is just as important to understand and map the human proteome as it was to map the human genome ~
some researchers might arque it is more important. At one time, people believed that each protein was
responsible for one, possibly two, tasks within the body. We now know that a single protein can be involved in
over 1000 tasks. This is of particular concern to pharmaceutical researchers. Many current pharmaceuticals are
designed to target and affect one or two proteins at most. Knowing that proteins work collectively, and in
complex ways, revealed the importance of re-thinking current methods of pharmaceutical development.

1 Define pharmaceuticals.

Barbara McClintock: Founder of cytogenetics

American scientist Barbara McClintock (1902-1992) provided indisputable, physical evidence that genes are
transposable. Her work proved that genetic material was exchanged between matching chromosomes and the
shuffling of genes produced the variation we recognise between related organisms. Barbara McClintock, 3
student of Thomas Hunt Morgan, is reported to have endured considerable ridicule from people who thought
she was wrong, in the 1930s, with the assistance of Harriet Creighton, she set about providing evidence for her

BOOK 2: GENETICS

Historic figures in genetics

Mendel

You will no doubt have heard of the botanist-monk Gregor Mendel (1822 - 1884) and his famous pea
experiments. Mende'’s observations of the different traits expressed by pea plants led to recognising that
each parent contributed heritable ‘units’ or ‘particles’ to their offspring.

Mendel studied seven characteristics of garden peas. Two of the most obvious contrasting characteristics he
used were the shape of seeds and the length of stems. He hand-pollinated the pea plants.

Mende! used statistics to help him realise that inherited characteristics are paired units. When he crossed pure
breeding tall plants with pure breeding short plants, all of the first generation (F;) offspring were tall. When
the F, generation were crossed with each other, the resulting second generation (F,) had a ratio of three tall
plants to every short plant.

1 Define trait.

2. Why would Mendel go to the bother of hand-pollinating pea plants when nature would have
done it for him?

3 Define statistics.
4 Give the genetic definition for pure breeding.

Mendel was unable to identify exactly what, or where, those units of inherited characteristics were found but
the realisation that the ‘units’ had to exist was a huge step forward in science. Prior to Mendel introducing this
concept, people had to rely on morphology and taxonomy when trying to work out species relationships. We
now recognise Mendet’s ‘units’ as genes, the basic units of inheritance, but it took time to narrow down exactly
what genes were and where genes were located,

5 Which branch of science does this define: ‘The study of the form and structure of organisms’?
6 Which branch of science does this define: The classification of plants and animals"?

BOOK 2: MEDICAL ETHICS

In vitro fertilisation

Not all couples that wish to have a baby are able to do so. About 15% of couples will experience difficulty in
trying to achieve a pregnancy. There are many reasons why a couple can be considered ‘infertile’, and
sometimes no cause for the infertility can be found.

1. Give two reasons why a male might be infertile.
2. Give two reasons why a female might be infertile.

The infertile couple has options. One of these is in vitro fertilisation, or IVF, a medical procedure to help
fertilisation. in vitro fertilisation — literally, ‘in-glass’ fertilisation ~ involves fertilisation of ova outside of the
body. Techniques vary, but the following shows a common sequence:

* Fertility drugs are given to the female to stimulate ova production.

* Ova are removed from the ovary by laparoscopic surgery, a minimally invasive technique that only involves
making a smail incision,

* The ova are placed in a glass container, sperm is added and they are incubated for about 24 hours for
fertilisation to take place.

* The fertilised eggs (zygotes) are transferred to a growth medium to ensure they can divide and grow
into embryos.

+ Embryos that develop normally are identified. A small number (two to four) are placed in the woman's
fallopian tube or can be implanted into the womb.

+ Embryos not used immediately may be frozen (in liquid nitrogen) for later use.

BOOK 2: GENETICS

Review of genetics terms

A thorough knowledge of the specialist terms used in Genetics is essential for an understanding of the subject.
Read this page carefully. Using the information given and a separate text book (or other source) write your own
definitions for the terms shown in italics,

The gene is the basic unit of inheritance for a given trait. Alleles are alternative forms of a gene.
For example genes can code for eye colour and the alleles include varying shades of brown, blue,
green and even violet.

‘A dominant allele produces a trait that overrides the presence of another trait (dominate to

control or rule). A capital (upper case) letter indicates dominant traits. For example, brown eyes are
a dominant trait over blue eyes. If an individual receives a brown (8) allele from its mother and a
brown from its father, the genotype is BB and brown eyes would be present. If the same individual
received a brown allele from its mother and a blue from its father, the genotype would be Bb and it
would still have brown eyes. The only way for the blue trait to appear is if It is the only one present
(bb). This is because the blue allele is recessive (meaning to recede or go back). A small (lower case)
letter indicates recessive traits.

Homo means ‘the same’ and homozygous allele pairs are the same, such as BB (meaning two
dominant, brown alleles) or bb (two recessive blues). Hetero means ‘different’ and heterozygous
allele pairs contain different alleles, such as Bb.

The genotype refers to the complete genetic make up of an individual whether or not it is
expressed. The phenotype describes what we see (from a Greek version of pheno, meaning ‘what
is seen). An individual may carry a Bb eye colour genotype. In other words one brown and one
blue eye colour allele. However, the phenotype will be brown. The brown eyes do not tell us if
the individual is homozygous dominant (88), meaning that both dominant alleles are present, or

BOOK 2; REPRODUCTION

Human reproduction II: Birth

‘An embryo obtains food and oxygen from the mother's blood via the placenta, which also removes waste.
The placenta forms on the wall of the uterus as the embryo develops. The placenta and embryo are joined
by the umbilical cord. The blood of the mother and baby do not meet or mix. The two blood supplies

are separate.
1 Will a baby necessarily have the same blood group as the mother?
Explain your answer.

The baby floats in a bag of liquid called the amniotic fluid. The
fluid acts as a shock absorber and protects the baby. It cushions the
baby from minor physical knocks the mother may receive. Samples
of the amniotic fluid containing cells of the unborn baby can be
used to check the sex of the child or for early detection of certain
disorders.

After about nine months the baby is usually fully developed and in
the correct position to be born. Hormones within the mother's
body signal the uterus to begin contractions, or /abour. These
contractions start to push the baby out.

The baby passes head-first, usually facedown, through the cervix

and down the vaginal canal. After the baby is born, the umbilical

cord is tied and cut. The navel, or belly button, is where the cord was attached. There are no nerves in the cord,
So it does not hurt the baby when the cord is severed. The placenta (or afterbirth) comes away from the mother
soon after the baby is born. It is checked for abnormalities and weighed (it should weigh about the same as the
baby, otherwise it may not have been fully expelled). It is then discarded, unless permission has been given to use
it for medical purposes, such as the extraction of stem cells.

Some babies are not in the upside-down position when they are ready to be born, These babies are either
born bottom first in a breech birth, which can cause injury to both mother and baby, or by caesarean section.

Reproduction in organisms

BOOK 2: REPRODUCTION

Reproduction in plants

Many plants reproduce sexually. in plants pollen is the male sex cell and ovum (plural ova) is the female sex cell.
Flowers are the organs of sexual reproduction in angiosperms (flowering plants). in sexual reproduction male
and female sex cells must come together. This process in plants is called pollination.

Flowers are highly modified shoots made up of four major parts. Sepals,
modified leaves, make up the outer series. The next inner series, the petals,
are also modified leaves which are usually not green but brightly coloured.
The third series consists of the stamens, the pollen-producing male portion of
the flower. A stamen is made up of an anther and a filament. The innermost
series are the carpels, female structures that produce the seeds. The stigma is
the top of the carpel and is sticky to catch pollen. Carpels can join to form a
structure called the pistil. The seeds of angiosperms develop in an ovary, a
part of the carpel that surrounds and protects the eqg-containing ovules.
Seeds develop from the ovules after pollination and fertilisation of the eggs.

BOOK 2: REPRODUCTION

The endocrine system

The endocrine system helps control our bodies by secreting (releasing) hormones from glands. Some hormones
only act on specific body parts, others cause a more general response. The principal controller of hormone
production is the hypothalamus (a part of the brain). The main glands concerned in reproduction are the
pituitary, testes and ovaries,

The pituitary is located at the base of the brain and is less than 1 cm in diameter and 0.5 g in mass. As welll as
releasing hormones that control growth and reproduction it manufactures others, which, in turn, control many
other glands.

The gonads are where gametes are produced. The male gonads are the testes and the female gonads are the
ovaries. Hormones from the pituitary gland and the steroid hormones from ovary or testis control reproductive
function in both sexes. In women, fluctuations of these hormones govern each menstrual cycle, stimulating
ovulation and preparing the uterus for pregnancy. The hypothalamus causes the pituitary gland to produce
gonadotropins — hormones that stimulate gonads.

The sex steroids also bring about the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In males, androgens
cause beard growth, deepening of the voice and increase in muscle size. Oestrogen and progesterone cause
breast development and the menstrual cycle in females. The male steroids are anabolic (building up) and
are among the banned substances that some athletes have used to encourage muscle development and
‘enhance performance.

FSH causes the formation of sperm in males and stimulates the development of ova in females. LH causes the
production of androgens in mates and for females stimulates ovulation. FSH starts off the menstrual cycle.

If a person is to survive and function properly, he or she must respond to changes in the environment.
Anything that causes a response from us is called a stimulus (plural stimuli). We detect stimuli from both inside

BOOK 2: THE SENSES

Sound and communication

Sound is a form of energy that requires a medium for propagation, ie it can travel through a gas, liquid or solid,
but not a vacuum. Vibrating objects produce sound. How quickly an object vibrates is called its frequency and is
measured in cycles per second or hertz (Hz).

High notes have high frequencies and are produced by rapidly vibrating objects. Low notes have low
frequencies and are produced by slowly vibrating objects. Pitch is the property of sound that we recognise
as lower and higher notes.

The wavelength of a sound wave is related to frequency (and pitch). The higher the frequency, the shorter

the wavelength. Wavelength is measured in metres.

a high frequency sound.

The larynx, lungs, tongue and lips all play a part in how humans produce intelligible (understandable) sounds.
The larynx (‘voice box’) is a hollow chamber near the top of the trachea (‘windpipe’) and contains the vocal
cords. The vocal cords are two pairs of folded mucous membranes. The larynx is supported by cartilage (qristle)
in places. Air passing from the lungs can cause the vocal cords to vibrate. The frequency of the sound is
controlled by muscles that change the length end tension of the vocal cords. An analogy (comparison) can

be made with the strings of a musical instrument that are plucked.

BOOK 2: THE SENSES

Vision II

The retina is a thin sheet of cells lining the inside of the eyeball which contains photoreceptors. Photoreceptors
are cells that contain light-sensitive pigments, such as rhodopsin. (A pigment is a substance that absorbs visible
light of a specific frequency and reflects visible light at a different wavelength, ie has a definite colour.) These
cells convert light images into electrochemical signals that are sent to the brain via the optic nerve for the brain
to interpret. These photoreceptors are of two main types: rods and cones. In an average human eye there will
be around 125 million rods and 6 million cones,

Rods are sensitive to blue-green light and are responsible for vision in dim light. They are more sensitive to
light than cones, but cannot distinguish between colours. Rods are connected in groups and cannot distinguish
fine detail.

Cones are responsible for colour vision. Colour blindness in humans is a result of certain colour-sensitive
pigments being missing from cones. Colour blindness can be inherited and pedigrees can be used to describe
how the condition is passed on, Cones can be individually connected to nerve fibres and give better visual acuity.

Nocturnal and diurnal animals have a different distribution of rods and cones, hence the difference in their
night and day vision. The greatest concentration of cones (and no rods) is at the fovea (central area of retina).
Concentration of rods decreases and concentration of cones increases towards the outer edges of the retina.

BOOK 3: DISEASE

Louis Pasteur and Sir Frank Macfarlane Burnet

Louis Pasteur

Louis Pasteur (1822-1895) was a pioneer in the search for the causes of disease in the second half of the
19th century. His work included:

+ how to kill bacteria in wine and beer without spoiling the flavour of the beverage
* disproving theory of ‘spontaneous generation’
* discovery of bacilli causing disease in silkworms
* discovery of inoculation against the bacteria that cause anthrax.
1. Define beverage.

Louis Pasteur was the founder of the science we now call microbiology. Microbiology is the study of microscopic
forms of life. in 1854 Pasteur moved to Lille, France, to take up a post at the local university. One of his projects
was to investigate why some beer and wine went sour - a problem that cost the French manufacturers of these
products a great deal of money. The manufacture of both beer and wine involves the changing of carbohydrates
into ethanol (alcohol) in a process called fermentation.

Pasteur examined many fermenting mixtures under the microscope and found different kinds of microbes. He
demonstrated that yeast was responsible for forming ethanol and that other microorganisms (bacteria) caused
the production of ethanoic (acetic) acid ~ the substance causing the sour taste. Vinegar, which is mainly ethanoic
acid, is named from the French ‘vinaigre’ meaning ‘sour wine’.

2. The bacteria causing ethanol to change to ethanoic acid are Acetobacter, a type of anaerobic bacteria.

Malaria

Insects can help or harm humans. Bees pollinate plants used for food but many other insects can harm human
health. When acting as disease-causing vectors, insects are harmful to humans and other animals. The female

insect that has caused the most death and suffering in human history. Female mosquitoes need blood to
produce eggs. In taking blood, the mosquito can pass on malaria to a person. This is called the mechanical
transfer of an infective agent. In this case, females inject sporozoites, a motile infective form of parasitic
protozoa that reproduce asexually in the new host.

infected person. The plasmodium finds its way into the mosquito when it bites someone infected with malaria.
The parasite flows into the mosquito along with the blood that is drawn up from the bite. It will then reach

mixes with saliva and anticoagulant used to ‘thin’ the blood of the host organism when it is bitten,

bites another human, the parasite will be injected into the person’s bloodstream. Once there, the parasite
migrates to the liver where it matures, replicates and causes a full-blown attack by infecting the red blood cells.

Prions

BOOK 3: DISEASE

Robert Koch

Robert Koch (1843-1910) was a German scientist who won the 1905 Nobel Prize for Medicine. He is regarded as
the co-founder (with Louis Pasteur) of modern microbiology. Koch is regarded as one of the greatest bacteriologists
the world has ever known. He had a wide range of interests, especially bacteriology, a science that was then in
its early stages. Koch’ first major finding in bacteriology was in 1876, when he demonstrated that if viable
Bacillus anthracis was injected into healthy mice, the mice eventually developed anthrax.

‘While many of the causes of disease are now recognised, in the past people did not realise (or refused to
believe) that tiny organisms could be responsible for certain illnesses. Koch was the first person to show
conclusively that the cause of an infectious disease was a specific organism. He was also able to identify
many of the organisms associated with particular diseases.

1. Define viable.
2. Suggest why people may not have believed that microorganisms were responsible for disease.

Koch was one of the first scientists to obtain microbes from infected animals and show how these microbes
could be grown in artificial conditions, The techniques he developed were used to isolate many different types
of bacteria. He also demonstrated the importance of being able to destroy the cultured microbes safely after
research had been carried out. Koch was one of the first people to advocate the sterilising of surgical instruments
with steam. Louis Pasteur also promoted the importance of sterilising surgical instruments, bedding and other
items used in hospitals.

3. Define sterilising.
4 Give an example of when bedding might need to be sterilised.

The body's defence system

Damaged cells (and white blood cells) secrete increased quantities of histamine, a hormone found in minute
quantities throughout the body. Histamine causes blood vessels to dilate, lowers blood pressure and makes
the capillary walls more permeable to fluids that need to move out of the small blood vessels to reach the
damaged tissue.

1. Define permeable.
2 Define dilate.
3 Define secrete.

The larger diameter of the blood vessels allows more liquid to flow. This in turn causes swelling (due to the
increased size of the blood vessels and extra fluid) and tension in stretched skin. The increase in temperature of
the inflamed area is due to increased blood flow - blood transfers heat around the body. There may also be an
increase in body temperature and pulse rate if a large area is affected. The increased temperature of the body is
a defence mechanism to make it harder for pathogens to survive. The swelling may also be painful and throb
due to the pulse from connected arteries, Pain is also caused by the release of certain chemicals by the body.

The increased circulation brings special defence agents to the site of cell damage. These include substances to.
ensure that blood clots in order to stop pathogens from circulating to the rest of the body. Macrophages
(histiocytes) are specialised types of white blood cells that are attracted to the damaged tissues. They are
phagocytes - they surround and digest dead tissue and foreign objects (such as pathogens) that enter the
bloodstream. The word comes from the Greek ‘phagos’ (one that eats) and ‘kytos’ (cell). Phagocytes can pass

BOOK 3: DISEASE

The role of white blood cells

There are five main types of white blood cells or leukocytes (leuko white/colourless, cyte cell). Ail leukocytes are
formed from stem cells present in bone marrow. Depending on the cell type, the leukocyte will either mature
while still in the bone marrow or, as in the case of the T-cells, they are formed in the bone marrow then travel
to the thymus to mature. (The thymus is situated near the breastbone/tracheal region.)

There are fewer white blood cells in the blood than red blood cells. It is estimated that they are outnumbered
by at least 700 to one. However, this does not mean they are found in small numbers! In fact, a conservative
estimate would number hundreds of millions (probably more) though many die within 24 hours. Once formed,
white blood cells begin circulating throughout blood, the lymph system and tissues.

When body tissue is damaged, chemicals are released that attract white blood cells to the site of the damage.
Invading bacteria also cause the release of chemicals that attract white blood cells. The primary role of all
leukocytes is to protect the body from invasion by disease-causing viruses and bacteria. White blood cells also
perform general housekeeping duties by digesting dead and dying cells and other unwanted matter found
within the body. The three main types of white blood cells are: granulocytes, monocytes and lymphocytes.

What is life?

Characteristics of living things

Most of us can recognise the difference between living and non-living things. Living organisms are identified
by a number of characteristics. They:

* move, or are in some way active (eg sessile (non-moving) organisms actively take up nutrients)
* have a recognisable size and shape (per species)
* respond to, and play an active role in, their external environment
* take up nutrients (organic compounds) from the environment
* reproduce (‘life arises from life’)
* have a reasonably predictable life span (eq die at a predictable ‘old age’ barring accident or early onset
of disease)
‘Life was never meant to be easy’ is a very common statement. Living organisms must fight to survive.
They do this using a number of means, including variation and adaptation.

4 division of labour. For example, sperm and eggs are specialised cells that are only involved in reproduction.

Behavioural adaptations to environment

The environment a species inhabits will affect how it adapts and evolves. Dispersion, or 'spreading-out’ activity,
plays an important role in many behavioural adaptations. Dispersion (disperse to part) can involve animals or
their food supply, For example, an animal that must travel long distances at regular intervals in order to eat will
need, among other characteristics, the strength and stamina to withstand the trips, Natural selection will favour
individuals who possess these features.

BOOK 3; ECOLOGY

Bioaccumulation and biomagnification

In the same way that nutrients and other compounds can be cycled through an ecosystem, so can harmful
toxins and pollutants, The terms bioaccumulation and biomagnification are often interchanged but each has
a specific meaning. Both words refer to the effects of pollutants (or toxins) entering the food chain. The
difference lies in their effects once they are present.

Bioaccumulation describes how substances enter the food chain at the lowest trophic level, in other words,
from the grazer upward to the final trophic level, the top carnivore. Bioaccumulation describes the
accumulation of an undesirable substance within the tissues of an organism or a population of organisms.

Biomagnification (sometimes called bioconcentration) describes the magnified effects, or increasing levels of
concentration, of these compounds as they travel along the food chain (trophic levels). Consider the simplified
example below used to illustrate how the amount of toxin can become biomagnified within an ecosystem:

A certain water bug is considered a pest in Lake Perfect. The water is treated with a toxic chemical
compound that kills most of the bugs. One molecule of poison is sufficient to kill each bug, therefore each
dead bug contains one molecule of the toxin.

Ten ‘mini-fish’ come along and each fish eats 50 poisoned bugs, The tissues of each mini-fish then contain
50 molecules of toxin. A large ‘killer fish’ then eats 10 of the mini-fish (each of which contains 50 molecules
of toxin). The tissues of the killer fish then contain 500 molecules of toxin.

A predatory bird eats 5 of the killer fish. Its tissues will contain 2500 molecules of toxin. A land carnivore kills
and eats 3 of the predatory birds (each of which has eaten 5 killer fish). The tissues of the land predator will
contain 7500 molecules of toxin.

BOOK 3: ECOLOGY

Components of an environment — biotic and abiotic

The biotic components of an environment are the organisms present.
1 What are the abiotic components of an environment?

For scientific purposes, the living world has been divided into groups called biomes, meaning ‘zone of life’.
Biomes are large, naturally occurring communities of plants and animals forming recognisable groups occupying
a large territory, The two major world biomes are aquatic and terrestrial. They can be divided into more specific
Categories based on the species present.

Aquatic (aqua, water): These are the ‘wet’ biomes and consist of freshwater (eg ponds, rivers) and marine (eg
sea/ocean, estuary). The composition of the water, which differs between each, affects the kinds of species that
will be found.

2 What is the main difference between freshwater and marine conditions?

Desert (desertare, to forsake): Roughly 20% of the Earth is desert. A biome that commonly receives less than
50 cm of precipitation per year is classified as a desert. This lack of water means that many types of vegetation
cannot survive and deserts are recognisable by the vast stretches of sand on which little or no vegetation is
present. Any vegetation present has evolved to adapt to the arid conditions,

Forest (forestis, wood): Forests are biomes that are densely covered by various tree species (depending on their
geographical location), Smaller trees and shrubs are usually found beneath the tree canopy. Forests cover about
30% of the Earth and represent 70% of the carbon found in living organisms,

and the Arctic districts of Europe, tundra are large, treeless areas. At ground level, the soil is cold and hard. As
expected, these are the most frigid of the biomes. Arctic tundra is found in the Northern Hemisphere (eg North

BOOK 3: ECOLOGY

Heavy metal pollution: the Minimata case

Mercury (chemical symbol Hq) is a ‘heavy metal’, one of a set of metal elements that are toxic. Mercury has
been used for thermometers, barometers, electrical switches, lighting, batteries and in the manufacture of
sodium hydroxide. The metal itself is moderately toxic, but becomes severely toxic when it forms compounds
with carbon.

Early last century, the people of the Japanese fishing village of Kumamoto, about 600 km from Tokyo, hoped
to expand their quiet little fishing village to a larger, more prosperous town. Consequently they welcomed
the arrival of the chemical producing company, Chisso Corporation. The Chisso plant produced, among other
forms of waste, mercury compounds that were freely dumped into Minimata Bay. The villagers depended on
this bay for fish. Almost immediately the deadly effects the chemicals had on the fish became evident. The
company recognised the damage and paid the villagers for permission to ruin their fishing industry. The
dumping of mercury compounds continued from the late 1920s up until 1968. Minimata Bay flowed out to
the Shiranui Sea (an inland sea), poisoning the aquatic species along its path.

By the 1950s rumours began to spread that the village was haunted by a spirit that took over the bodies of
Kumamoto residents, Many cats, and some dogs, began to do ‘weird dances’ on the streets before dropping
dead, Children were also behaving strangely and soon adults followed. People began to develop speech and
vision problems, others began screaming wildly, muscle spasms led to paralysis and suicides occurred. The
bizarre condition became known as ‘Minimata Disease’.

People then suspected some form of infectious disease was attacking the central nervous system. The corporation’s
doctor, Dr Hajim Hosokawa, discovered the connection between a fish diet and the condition. This led him to
analyse the fish and identify the heavy mercury contamination.

BOOK 3: ECOLOGY

Parasitism, mutualism and commensalism

Relationships between organisms take several forms. Symbiosis is the term used to describe how different
plant or animal species live together. The effects of the relationship are then classified as parasitism,
mutualism or commensalism.

Parasitism

The word parasite comes from an old word meaning ‘one who eats at another's table’. A parasite is an
organism that obtains its nutrients by living in or on another organism. The parasite obtains nutrients at the
expense of the host organism it associates with. Thus, parasitism involves one organism depriving another of its
nutrition, In this case, the parasite benefits and the host suffers. An example of a parasitic relationship is the
tapeworm. Tapeworms can infect humans and other animals, living in the alimentary canal of the host. The
tapeworm takes much of the nutrients its host ingests, leaving the host undernourished as a result (and in
extreme cases, dead),

Mutualism

As the name suggests, mutualism involves a relationship that is of mutual benefit to both organisms. A well-
known case of mutualism involves various species of birds living on or near larger animals, such as horses, cows,
thins and giraffes. The birds eat the tiny bugs that would otherwise irritate or damage the skin of the larger
animal. in exchange for providing this easy meal, the larger animal benefits by having its body kept free of
pests, Similar examples occur in the oceans with smaller fish performing the same task on larger species. For
example, a remora is a fish that has a disk on its head, which it uses like a sucker to cling onto other fishes,
especially sharks. Remoras feed on food scraps left over by their hosts or on parasites of the host. They can also
swim alone and have been seen clinging to the hulls of ships.

OOK 3: PALAEONTOLOGY

Fossils reviewed

Palaeontology is the science of fossils (paleo ancient). A fossil can be defined as any
trace of a plant or animal that has been preserved in the Earth’s crust, most
‘commonly in rock or sand, Fossils can be formed as imprints, skeletal remains or by
an organism being petrified. Often only the hard parts of organisms (living things),
for example bones, shell or bark tend to be preserved.

A fossil can be made from a porous (contains lots of small holes) object such as a
bone. Under the right conditions water containing minerals can fill the porous parts.
Over a long period of time this can make the object resemble stone and preserves it.
In @ similar way, a piece of wood can have its molecules replaced very slowly by
minerals, making it petrified.

Fossils form when materiats from the Earth’s crust (sediment) cover the remains of an organism, either under
water or on land. As greater amounts of deposit accumulate, the remains are compressed by the rock. Imprints
(perhaps a footprint in soft soil) can also be filled in and covered up over time.

Various scientific tests can be performed to determine the ages of fossils, thus enabling us to develop theories
as to how life on Earth evolved. Not only does finding a certain species in a given area suggest what lived there
(and when), but it can also tell us about environmental conditions, For example, fossilised shells have been
found in deserts suggesting that water once covered the land.

Homo sapiens

A species is made up of related organisms capable of interbreeding. They have a two-part name: the genus
(first letter capitalised), then a Latin species name (no capitals). Scientists classify all humans currently living on
Earth as members of a single species, Homo sapiens. The list below shows how we can classify Homo sapiens
based on anatomical features:

+ kingdom Animalia ~ an animal

+ phylum Chordata - with a backbone

+ subphylum Vertebrata - segmented spinal column

‘+ class Mammalia ~ suckles its young

* subclass Eutheria — offspring develop with a placenta

* order Primate - hands/feet with five digits and two mammary glands on the chest
+ suborder Anthropoidea — stereoscopic vision and a proportionately large brain

* family Hominidae

The primates that most closely resemble humans are chimpanzees, gorillas and orang-utans. Skeletons of Homo
sapiens differ from these because of a very early adaptation to standing upright (erect posture) and walking on
two feet (bipedalism). Humans have an S-shaped spinal column, putting the centre of gravity of the human
body directly above the feet. This, and the modified pelvic region, makes walking upright easier.

Other anthropoids can walk upright to a limited extent, however, they all have spines which are straight or
arched. They also have prehensile (grasping) feet and use their front limbs (hands) to lean on when walking.
Because humans walk completely upright, hands have become much more developed, for example the thumb
is fully opposable to the other fingers. Thus hands are able to make and manipulate tools. Tools were first

Primates

Researchers are divided as to exactly when the primates first appeared on Earth. Some believe they evolved
from an insectivorous ancestry during the late Cretaceous (135-70 million years ago) period. Others date the
first primates at the Palaeocene (65-54 million years ago) period. Either way, the earliest primates were here
a long time ago.

Primate groups

There are two divisions of primates. They are the prosimians (Prosimii - pro before, simian apelike) and the
anthropoids (Anthropoidea, resembling man), There are five families of the older prosimii, or ‘Old World’
primates, most of which are found in Africa, the Philippines and Madagascar. Examples of prosimians are the
lemur, tarsier (related to the lemur), loris, and the tree shrew.

Primates are animals, which belong to the mammalian order primates.

The anthropoids include the monkeys, apes and humans. Their faces are generally much flatter than the
prosimians and they have two premolar teeth, Anthropoids also have areas on their faces and/or bodies that are
not covered by hair. They can sit in an upright position - or at least on their haunches (the area consisting of the
thighs and buttocks). Anthropoids use their opposable thumbs and grasping hands to hold objects and aid in
climbing. Depending on the species, they can walk either completely, or for short periods, using bipedal (two-
legged) motion. Apes lack a tail,

arboreal and lack opposable thumbs, tending to use their prehensile tail to grasp (prehensile to seize). New
World anthropoids walk using their arms and legs (quadrapedal). They have three premolars, as opposed to the
pair found in anthropoids.

BOOK 3: PALAEONTOLOGY

Vertebrate evolution

Before you attempt this section, remind yourself of the following classification terms.
Class, Family, Genus, Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Species
1 Rewrite them in order, from the least specific to the most specific.

‘Many species in the phylum Chordata are considered the most advanced of animals.
it was long believed that the chordates evolved from the Echinoderms, meaning
‘spiny skinned animal’ (eq starfish). However, most scientists now believe the two
groups co-evolved from a different, common ancestor. Since most of the early
chordates were soft-bodied and believed to have arisen about 700 million years ago
(during the Pre-Cambrian era), it is near impossible to find fossil evidence to confirm
what embryonic development patterns suggest about their relationship.

2) What does co-evolve mean?

A distinguishing feature that separates the first vertebrates from the chordates is the presence of a notochord
at some point during development, The notochord is a collagen-based rod that strengthens the dorsal (back)
part of an animal and develops into a vertebral column (backbone). Collagen is a fibrous protein that can make
up connective tissue. The notochord commonly extends from the tail to the head and, as the animal develops, it
is replaced with the vertebral column. The original chordates were believed to be slender, soft-bodied, filter-
feeding animals. The earliest chordates were the ancestors of the vertebrates. The first vertebrate form was the

THE PERIODIC TABLE

Lavoisier took the first step in classifying elements in 1789. He divided

the twenty-five or thirty elements known to him into metals and non pe genoale Gane cases
metals. In 1829 Johann Dobereiner noticed that where groups of three oF increasing atomic number,
similar elements (triads) occurred, the relative atomic mass of the .
middle element came approximately between those of the other two. However, for many elements the
idea did not work. In 1864 John Newlands found that if the elements known to science at the time were
arranged in order of increasing relative atomic masses, a pattern emerged. Starting at any element, every
eighth element was ‘a kind of repetition of the first’. Because of the similarity of this pattern to the
musical scale, he called it the law of octaves. This ‘law’ is not very reliable,

1 Explain the difference between atomic mass and atomic number.

In 1869 Dmitri Mendeléev (or Mendeléeff) made a breakthrough. He arranged the elements in order of
increasing relative atomic masses in a similar way to Newlands but, in order to obtain a better repetition,
he left gaps for elements which he assumed must exist but had not yet been discovered. He found that
many properties then followed a repeating pattern, or periodic variation.

Not only did Mendeléev have to leave gaps for undiscovered elements, he also had to correct some
relative atomic masses that had been determined erroneously to make the elements fit into the right
groups, Mendeléev predicted the existences of 21 missing elements including ‘eka-silicon’ which is now
named germanium. His predicted chemical and physical properties were very close to those actually
found when germanium was discovered.

The Periodic Table we now use lists the elements in order
of atomic number (not atomic mass). Figure 1 shows an
outline of the Periodic Table. There are just over 90
naturally occurring elements.

Chemistry is a science that studies the composition and properties of substances and how those
substances interact and transform to create new substances. Physical changes involve the changing of a
substance from one state to another without altering the chemical nature of the substance. For example,

relatively easy to reverse the change.

Only the noble gases exist as discrete (separate) atoms. Imagine that a complete outer shell of electrons
forms a kind of ‘case’ around the atom. Then think of that case as complete and enclosing the whole

configuration of the noble gases. The type of bonding present in a compound will affect its properties

parent atoms, This is because they now have a different electronic structure to the parent atom and
therefore different chemical properties. lonic compounds are generally solids (often crystalline).

valence (outer) electrons, leaving out the inner shells of electrons. Therefore, there may be many more
electrons present but the ‘inner’ levels are not illustrated.

METALS AND METALLIC BONDING Bp

Metals can be recognised by their characteristic physical properties.
1 Name three typical properties of metals,

Metals form two types of bonds: ionic bonds and metallic bonds. They form ionic bonds with non-
metals. In ionic bonding, metals obtain noble gas electron structure by transferring electrons to non-
metals.

2 What type of ions are formed by metals in ionic bonds?

In metals, the bonding between atoms is often strong. Metal structures contain billions of atoms packed
together very tightly. The atoms are packed together in simple structures. These patterns can be
modelled by dropping many marbles into a small box. Many metals are dense; they have atoms that are
heavy and pack closely together. When metal atoms bond together, they do not form a noble gas type

structure.

are different from covalent bonds in one important way.
In a covalent bond, the electrons spend their time between
the two atoms that are bonded, When metal atoms share
their electrons, these electrons are free to move anywhere e
within the metal structure. There is a ‘sea of electrons’
surrounding the positive metal cations (see figure 1).
Another way to visualise this is to imagine metals as three-
dimensional lattices of positive ions in a ‘sea’ of valence
electrons, The delocalised outer-shell electrons in the lattice
are extremely mobile and can readily move through the = pasta Seas
lattice when excited by either thermal or electrical energy.
Metallic bonding is strong; hence metals are often hard and have high melting points. However, layers
in the metal lattice can be forced to ‘slip over’ each other; this accounts for the malleability and ductility
of metals. Mixtures of different metals are called alloys.

NAMING COMPOUNDS

If a compound contains only two elements its name usually ends in ‘-ide’. In a compound that contains
a metal and a non-metal, the metal comes first in the compound’s name. For example, iron (III) oxide,
Fe,O,, contains the metal iron, Fe, and the non-metal oxygen, O. Sodium chloride (NaCl) contains the
metal sodium, Na, and the non-metal chlorine, Cl.

These are some name changes for elements present in compounds:
F, fluorine — fluoride I, iodine — iodide Br, bromine — bromide
O, oxygen ~ oxide N, nitrogen — nitride S, sulfur — sulfide

Often in chemistry atoms form groups that stay together during reactions, acting in a similar way to a
single atom. For example, when four oxygen atoms bond with a sulfur atom, a sulfate ion, SO,*, is
formed. Now consider magnesium sulfate (MgSO,) in a reaction, This compound can ‘break up’ to
form a magnesium ion (Mg”) and a sulfate ‘unit’ with the five atoms that form the sulfate unit
remaining intact. A group of atoms that stays together in chemical reactions is called a radical. If
more than two elements are present in a compound and one of these is oxygen, then the compound's
name usually ends in ‘-ate’. These radicals (groups of atoms) are common parts of compounds:

SO, = sulfate -CO, = carbonate -NO,= nitrate -PO, = phosphate

Naming compounds that contain radicals is not as confusing as it may first appear. The metals keep

most (or a recognisable part) of their names and the presence of oxygen in the radical group usually
denotes an ‘-ate’ ending to the name.

VALENCY AND FORMULA

Atoms in chemical compounds have a characteristic combining power or valency. This involves the
number of electrons in an incomplete outer shell and can be defined in several ways:

* It represents the charge on an ion

* It is equal to the number of electron pairs shared in a molecule

* It is the number of electrons transferred when forming an ion.
1 Use your own textbook to find an alternative definition for valency.

For elements in Groups I II, Ill, IV and 0, the group valency is the same as the group number (e.g. Group
1 elements have a valency of 1). For elements in Groups V, VI & VII there are two group valencies. One is
the same as the group number and the other more likely valency is 8 minus the group number.
